title: 〜ということ (nominalizer)
meaning: Add 「ということ」 after a sentence to turn the whole thing into a noun: “the fact that ...”.
connection: Plain-form sentence + ということ (after nouns and な-adjectives, 「だ」 is usually added)

senses.label: Turning content into a noun
senses.meaning: Turns the content of a statement into a noun, followed by 「が／を／は」. Often the object of 「わかる」「知る」「聞く」「忘れる」. It puts more focus on the content itself than plain 「こと」.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + ということ + が／を／は (〜ということがわかる／〜ということを知る)
examples: I really came to understand that Japanese honorifics are difficult.
Today I heard for the first time that he quit the company.
Please don't forget that health is the most important thing.

senses.label: Checking what someone means
senses.meaning: 「〜ということですか／ということですね」 checks what the other person means: “So you mean ..., right?” Often paired with 「つまり」.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + ということですか／ということですね (casual: 〜ってこと？)
examples: So tomorrow is a day off, right?
Does that mean I don't have to go?
So we can't meet today?

senses.label: Explaining what something means
senses.meaning: 「AとはBということだ」 or 「AというのはBということだ」 explains what a word or thing means. Fairly formal.
senses.connection: Noun + とは／というのは + plain-form sentence + ということだ
examples: “Independence” means living by your own efforts.
Working means taking on responsibility.

notes: After nouns and な-adjectives, adding 「だ」 is more standard: 「学生だということ」「便利だということ」.
In casual speech it often shrinks to 「〜ってこと」: 「明日休みってこと？」.
Sentence-final 「〜ということだ」 for hearsay or conclusions is a separate N3 pattern. Use context to tell them apart.

daily.title: Passing on news
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about someone's news, treating what you heard as one topic.
daily.example: Did you know that Tanaka is getting married?

daily.title: Confirming plans
daily.description: Wrapping up plans with a friend by checking the time and place.
daily.example: So we're meeting at the station at ten, right?

work.title: Confirming a decision in a meeting
work.description: Near the end of a meeting, checking the decision with everyone.
work.example: So, is it all right if we submit the materials by next week?

work.title: Explaining in a business email
work.description: Explaining a change to a client and asking for their understanding.
work.example: Please note that the delivery will be delayed by one week.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」 + the verb 「いう（言う）」 + the formal noun 「こと」. It originally meant “the thing described as ...”. Over time 「という」 lost its meaning of “say” and now simply links the content to a noun, so it's usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: 「こと」 can also attach directly to a plain-form sentence, as in 「泳ぐことが好きだ」. 「ということ」 stresses the content and is common as the object of knowing, hearing or understanding. For the action itself, use 「こと」.

similar.title: 〜の (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: 「の」 is used for perception and concrete actions (「歌うのを聞いた」). 「ということ」 is for abstract facts and information, and can't go with perception verbs like 「見る・聞こえる」.

similar.title: 〜ということだ (hearsay/conclusion)
similar.explanation: Sentence-final 「〜ということだ」 means “I hear that ...” or “in other words ...”; it's an N3 pattern. In this entry, the content is turned into a noun and followed by a particle.

similar.title: 〜という意味だ
similar.explanation: 「という意味だ」 only explains what a word means. 「ということだ」 can also explain what a situation implies.

title: 〜は〜が、〜は〜 (contrast)
meaning: Two 「は」 set two things side by side for contrast: “A is ..., but B is ...”.
connection: Noun A は + predicate + が (けど)、noun B は + predicate

senses.label: Contrast with “but”
senses.meaning: 「が／けど」 joins the two clauses, and the two 「は」 create a sharp contrast. The focus is on how the two differ.
senses.connection: Noun は + predicate + が／けど、noun は + predicate
examples: I eat meat, but I don't eat fish.
My older brother is tall, but my younger brother is short.
Weekdays are busy, but weekends are free.

senses.label: Side-by-side contrast
senses.meaning: Pauses with the te-form or the 〜く／〜で form to list the differences objectively. Softer than 「が」.
senses.connection: Noun は + predicate in te-form／〜く／〜で、noun は + predicate
examples: Summers are hot and winters are cold.
My older sister is a doctor, and my younger sister is a lawyer.

senses.label: Leaving the second half unsaid
senses.meaning: Only 「Aは〜が」 is said and the rest is left out. It hints “but not the other things”, softening the statement.
senses.connection: Noun は + predicate + が……／けど……
examples: I can read hiragana, but...
I can drink a little alcohol, but...

notes: Words marked by 「が」 or 「を」 switch to 「は」 when contrasted: 「肉を食べる」→「肉は食べる」.
After particles like 「に・で・と・から」, just add 「は」: 「東京には行ったが、大阪には行っていない」.
Even a single 「は」 can imply contrast: 「ビールは飲みます」 suggests “but not other drinks”.

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Telling a friend about family members' different habits.
daily.example: My father drinks, but my mother doesn't.

daily.title: Explaining food preferences
daily.description: When a friend treats you to a meal, you explain what you can and can't eat.
daily.example: Spicy food is fine, but I'm not big on sweets.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Comparing two cities while watching the forecast.
daily.example: It's sunny in Tokyo, but rainy in Osaka.

work.title: Reporting progress
work.description: Telling your boss how each task is going.
work.example: Task A is done, but task B isn't finished yet.

work.title: Comparing proposals
work.description: Comparing the pros and cons of two plans in a meeting.
work.example: Plan A costs less, but Plan B offers higher quality.

etymology: The binding particle 「は」 originally picked out one thing from many to talk about, so it naturally carries a sense of contrast. With two 「は」 in one sentence, the contrast is at its clearest.

similar.title: 〜は (topic)
similar.explanation: A single 「は」 mainly marks the topic. This pattern uses two 「は」 to highlight a contrast.

similar.title: 〜が (but)
similar.explanation: 「が」 alone just joins two clauses with “but”. Only with two 「は」 does it become a full “A is ..., but B is ...” contrast.

similar.title: 〜も (also)
similar.explanation: 「も」 says two things are the same (「AもBも好きだ」). Contrastive 「は」 says they're different.

title: 〜ございます (polite form of ある)
meaning: A very polite form of 「あります」, meaning “there is / to have”. Used by shop staff and receptionists, in announcements and in other polite settings.
connection: Noun + が／は + ございます; い-adjective with う sound change + ございます

senses.label: There is / to have (polite)
senses.meaning: The polite equivalent of 「あります」, used when speaking to customers or superiors. Only for things that exist or are owned; for people, use 「おります」 or 「いらっしゃいます」.
senses.connection: Noun が／は + ございます／ございません／ございました
examples: The restroom is on the second floor.
Do you have any questions?
We're very sorry. That item is currently out of stock.

senses.label: Set greetings
senses.meaning: Before 「ございます」, adjectives go through a う sound change: ありがたい→ありがとう, おめでたい→おめでとう, はやい→おはよう. These have become fixed greetings.
senses.connection: い-adjective with う sound change + ございます (ありがとうございます／おめでとうございます)
examples: Thank you, as always.
Congratulations on your marriage.
Good morning.

notes: 「でございます」 is the polite form of 「です」 (「こちらは会議室でございます」). It's different from this entry, which replaces 「あります」.
Don't use 「ございます」 for people: ✕「田中はございません」. Say 「田中はおりません」.
Common in department stores, hotels and customer service. Not used between friends.
「〜はございますか」 is much more polite than 「ありますか」 and is a standard phrase for shop staff.

daily.title: At a clothing store
daily.description: A customer asks about other sizes, and the clerk answers politely.
daily.example: We have it in medium too.

daily.title: Hotel front desk
daily.description: The receptionist tells a guest where breakfast is served.
daily.example: Breakfast is served at the restaurant on the first floor.

daily.title: Birthday wishes
daily.description: Politely wishing a happy birthday to someone older or someone you're not close to.
daily.example: Happy birthday.

work.title: Welcoming a client
work.description: Asking a visiting client what they'd like to drink.
work.example: We have coffee and tea. Which would you prefer?

work.title: Closing a meeting
work.description: The chair checks for any final comments.
work.example: Are there any other comments?

etymology: From 「御座ある（ござある）」, shortened to 「ござる」. Adding the polite auxiliary 「ます」 gave 「ござります」, which later became 「ございます」. 「御座」 originally meant the seat of a noble person, and came to mean “(a noble person) is present / exists”.

similar.title: 〜でございます
similar.explanation: 「でございます」 equals 「です」 (“to be”). The 「ございます」 in this entry equals 「あります」 (“there is / to have”).

similar.title: 〜がある・〜がいる (existence)
similar.explanation: 「あります」 is ordinary polite speech. 「ございます」 is more formal and common in service jobs and formal settings.

similar.title: 参る・申す・いたす (special humble verbs)
similar.explanation: For people, use humble 「おります」, as in 「担当者がおります」. 「ございます」 is only for things and matters.

title: 〜 (plain-form clause) + noun (noun modification)
meaning: A plain-form clause goes directly before a noun to describe it, like an English relative clause (“the book that I bought”).
connection: Plain-form clause (verb, adjective, noun + だった, etc.) + noun

senses.label: Verb clauses
senses.meaning: Plain verb forms (dictionary form, た-form, ない-form, ている-form) go directly before the noun. No 「の」 is added, and nothing like “that” or “which” is needed.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + noun (買った本／来ない人／住んでいる町)
examples: The book I bought yesterday is really interesting.
Anyone who isn't coming to the party, please let me know.
The town where I live is quiet.

senses.label: Adjective and noun clauses
senses.meaning: い-adjectives go directly before the noun; な-adjectives take 「な」. Noun predicates use 「の」 in the present and 「だった」 in the past.
senses.connection: い-adjective + noun／な-adjective な + noun／noun の・noun だった + noun
examples: A girl with big eyes is laughing.
I listened to a song I loved as a child.
I want to live in a town with good transportation.

senses.label: が→の inside the clause
senses.meaning: The subject marker 「が」 inside a modifying clause can change to 「の」. This only works inside a clause that modifies a noun.
senses.connection: Noun の + verb + noun (母の作った料理)
examples: The food my mother makes is the best.
I read a novel my friend wrote.

notes: Don't use 「です・ます」 inside the clause: ✕「昨日買いました本」→「昨日買った本」.
The subject inside the clause takes 「が」 or 「の」, not 「は」: ✕「私は作ったケーキ」→「私が作ったケーキ」.
Present-tense nouns take 「の」, not 「だ」: 「父が医者の友だち」, ✕「父が医者だ友だち」.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a friend from university to your family.
daily.example: This is a friend I met at university.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: Talking to yourself while looking for the umbrella you just bought.
daily.example: Where did I put the umbrella I bought yesterday?

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Recommending the ramen shop in front of the station to a friend.
daily.example: The ramen at the shop in front of the station is really good.

work.title: Following up by email
work.description: Reminding a client to look at materials you sent earlier.
work.example: Please take a look at the materials we sent last week.

work.title: Introducing a product
work.description: Presenting a popular product to a client.
work.example: This product is popular with young people.

etymology: 「連体修飾」 is a Japanese grammar term: 「連体」 means “linking to a noun (体言)” and 「修飾」 means “modification”. In Japanese, modifiers always come first, so a modifying clause always comes before the noun it describes.

similar.title: 〜 (verb plain form) + noun (relative clause)
similar.explanation: At N5 you mainly learn verb plain forms before nouns. This entry extends that to adjectives, noun clauses and the が→の switch.

similar.title: 〜の (replacing が in a relative clause)
similar.explanation: Covers only the switch from 「が」 to 「の」 inside a modifying clause, which is one part of this entry.

similar.title: 〜な + noun (na-adjectives before nouns)
similar.explanation: A single な-adjective modifying a noun. This entry is about a whole clause, with its own subject, object and so on, modifying a noun.

title: 〜をしている (appearance/features)
meaning: 「Modifier + noun + をしている」 describes lasting features of people or things, such as their looks, shape or color.
connection: Adjective or other modifier + 目・髪・顔・形・色, etc. + をしている

senses.label: Describing looks
senses.meaning: Describes natural, lasting features of a person or animal. A modifier such as an adjective is required. The 「〜ている」 form shows a state.
senses.connection: Modifier + 目・髪・顔・声・体 + をしている／をしています
examples: She has long hair.
This cat has blue eyes.
My older brother has a sturdy build.

senses.label: Describing shape and color
senses.meaning: Can also describe the shape, color and other visible features of objects.
senses.connection: Modifier + 形・色 + をしている
examples: This stone is shaped like a heart.
The evening sky was a beautiful color.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: Before a noun, 「〜をした + noun」 is common. 「〜をしている + noun」 also works.
senses.connection: Modifier + 目・顔, etc. + をした + noun
examples: A man with a red face came in.
A child with big eyes is waving.

notes: A modifier is required: ✕「彼は目をしている」. Say 「きれいな目をしている」.
To describe a state at the end of a sentence, use 「〜をしている」, not 「〜をする」: ✕「彼女は長い髪をする」.
「彼女は髪が長い」 means almost the same. 「〜をしている」 focuses more on the overall look.

daily.title: Looking for a lost child
daily.description: Describing a child to a staff member.
daily.example: He's a boy with short hair, wearing a white shirt.

daily.title: Talking about pets
daily.description: Telling a friend about your dog.
daily.example: Our dog has brown fur.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Common when novels describe what a character looks like.
daily.example: The old man had sad eyes.

work.title: Describing a product
work.description: Explaining a product's shape to a customer.
work.example: This product is round, so it's easy to hold.

etymology: Besides “do”, the verb 「する」 can mean “to have a certain look or state”, as in 「青い顔をする」. One theory is that this comes from “showing a certain appearance”. 「ている」 shows that the state continues.

similar.title: 〜は〜が〜 (double subject)
similar.explanation: 「彼女は髪が長い」 makes “long” the predicate. 「彼女は長い髪をしている」 presents “long hair” as an overall feature. The meanings are close.

similar.title: 〜がする (sensation)
similar.explanation: 「いい匂いがする」 is about smells and sounds you sense. 「〜をしている」 is about visible appearance.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: Ordinary 「〜をしている」 means “is doing ...” (「宿題をしている」). In this entry it describes appearance, after nouns like body parts, shapes and colors.

title: 〜くは (adjective + は, contrastive negation)
meaning: Adding 「は」 after the く-form of an い-adjective softens a negative or adds contrast: “not exactly ...”, “it is ..., but ...”.
connection: い-adjective stem + くは + ない／ありません／ある

senses.label: Softened negative
senses.meaning: 「〜くはない」 sounds softer than 「〜くない」: “not really ...”. It often implies “but in other ways ...”.
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + くはない／くはありません (よい→よくはない)
examples: This room isn't big, but it's very clean.
This dish isn't bad, but it's not especially good either.
The price isn't that high.

senses.label: Past: くはなかった
senses.meaning: 「〜くはなかった」 looks back on the past: “it wasn't (as ... as expected)”. Often used with 「思ったほど」.
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + くはなかった／くはありませんでした
examples: The exam wasn't as hard as I thought.
It wasn't really cold yesterday.

senses.label: Concession: くはある
senses.meaning: 「〜くはあるが」 first admits “it is ..., true”, then turns to the other side. Somewhat formal.
senses.connection: い-adjective stem + くはある／くはあります + が／けど
examples: This bag is heavy, but it's sturdy and will last a long time.
It's certainly cheap, but I'm worried about the quality.

notes: 「いい」 conjugates from 「よい」: 「よくはない」, not ✕「いくはない」.
For な-adjectives and nouns, the equivalent is 「〜ではない」: 「静かではない」「上手ではない」.
Often paired with 「〜くもない」: 「高くもなく、安くもない」 (neither expensive nor cheap).

daily.title: A friend asks your opinion
daily.description: A friend asks if the food is good, and you gently say it's okay.
daily.example: It's not bad. It's a bit spicy, though.

daily.title: Hesitating while shopping
daily.description: You like something in a store but can't decide.
daily.example: It's not expensive, but I don't think I need it right now.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Telling your family about the weather as you head out.
daily.example: It's not cold today, but it's really windy.

work.title: Evaluating a proposal
work.description: Objectively weighing a plan's pros and cons in a meeting.
work.example: The cost isn't low, but we can expect good results.

etymology: Formed from the adjective's 「〜く」 form plus the binding particle 「は」. 「は」 highlights and contrasts, limiting the negation to that one adjective. This softens the tone or suggests that “other aspects are a different story”.

similar.title: 〜くない (i-adjective negative)
similar.explanation: 「〜くない」 is a direct negative. Adding 「は」 in 「〜くはない」 softens it and hints at other aspects.

similar.title: 〜ないことはない
similar.explanation: 「ないことはない」 is a partial yes: “it's not that it isn't ...”. 「〜くはない」 is a softened negative.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: 「わけではない」 denies a conclusion the listener might draw (“it's not that ...”). 「〜くはない」 just softens the negation of the adjective itself.

similar.title: 〜は〜が、〜は〜 (contrast)
similar.explanation: Both use the contrastive power of 「は」. In 「〜くはない」, 「は」 comes right after the adjective.

meaning: 「こんな・そんな・あんな・どんな」 come before a noun to describe its nature or type: “this kind of / that kind of / what kind of”.
connection: こんな／そんな／あんな／どんな + noun; 〜に + adjective/verb

senses.label: This kind / that kind
senses.meaning: 「こんな」 points to something near the speaker, 「そんな」 to something near the listener or just mentioned by them, and 「あんな」 to something far away or remembered by both. They describe nature or type, often with emotion and sometimes negatively.
senses.connection: こんな／そんな／あんな + noun (こんな本／そんなこと)
examples: I've always wanted a book like this.
Don't say things like that.
I never want to see someone like that again.

senses.label: What kind of
senses.meaning: 「どんな」 asks about the nature or type of something: “what kind of”.
senses.connection: どんな + noun + か (どんな人／どんな音楽)
examples: What kind of music do you like?
What's the new teacher like?

senses.label: This much / that much
senses.meaning: With 「に」, they become adverbs of degree: 「こんなに」 “this much”, 「そんなに〜ない」 “not that ...”, 「どんなに〜ても」 “no matter how ...”.
senses.connection: こんなに／そんなに／あんなに／どんなに + adjective/verb
examples: This is the first time I've had such a delicious cake.
The test wasn't that hard.
No matter how busy I am, I always eat breakfast.

senses.label: Not at all
senses.meaning: 「そんなことない」 denies what the other person said, especially as a modest reply to a compliment: “Oh no, not at all.”
senses.connection: そんなこと(は)ない／ありません
examples: Oh no, not at all.
That's not true.

notes: 「こんな」 attaches directly to a noun, with no 「の」: ✕「こんなの本」. On its own, 「こんなの」 means “something like this”.
「この本」 is this specific book; 「こんな本」 is this type of book.
In speech, 「こんな・そんな・あんな」 often express surprise or disapproval. In formal settings, use 「このような・そのような」.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: Showing a clerk a photo and asking for something similar.
daily.example: Do you have any shirts with a design like this?

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is upset over a small mistake.
daily.example: Don't worry about it so much.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Getting to know someone you've just met.
daily.example: What do you do on your days off?

work.title: Job interview
work.description: The interviewer asks about the applicant's experience.
work.example: What did you work hard at as a student?

work.title: Helping a customer
work.description: A clerk asks what the customer needs.
work.example: What kind of item are you looking for?

etymology: One theory says they're contractions of 「このような・そのような・あのような・どのような」. Another says they come from 「こ・そ・あ・ど」 plus 「なる」, the attributive form of the old copula 「なり」, with a sound change. Adding 「に」 makes adverbs like 「こんなに」.

similar.title: 〜この・その・あの・どの + noun
similar.explanation: 「この」 points to one specific thing; 「こんな」 is about nature or type. 「この本」 is “this book”; 「こんな本」 is “a book like this”.

similar.title: 〜ような・〜ように・〜みたいな (comparison, examples)
similar.explanation: 「このような」 is the formal version of 「こんな」, used mostly in writing and formal settings.

similar.title: こういう・そういう・ああいう・どういう
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「こんな」 and its set, but more neutral and less emotional. 「どういう」 can also ask “what does that mean?” (「どういうことですか」).

meaning: Says that something is one member of a group: “A is one of the B”.
connection: Noun A + は + noun B (the whole group) + の一つだ

senses.label: A is one of B
senses.meaning: Places the topic in a category as one of its members. Modifiers like 「有名な」「代表的な」「好きな」 often come before B.
senses.connection: AはBの一つだ／の一つです (B is a group with several members)
examples: Kyoto is one of Japan's most popular tourist destinations.
Sushi is one of Japan's signature dishes.
This is one of my favorite movies.

senses.label: One of them is ...
senses.meaning: Names the category first, then one of its members. Often used to explain reasons, problems or features.
senses.connection: Bの一つに + Aがある／Bの一つは + Aだ
examples: Tea ceremony is one of Japan's traditional arts.
One of the reasons it failed was poor preparation.

senses.label: As one of ...
senses.meaning: 「Bの一つとして」 means “as one of B”, followed by an action or evaluation.
senses.connection: Bの一つとして + verb
examples: As one of my healthy habits, I take a walk every morning.
This temple is listed as one of the World Heritage Sites.

notes: Just like English “one of the most ...”, Japanese can say 「最も〜の一つ」: 「最も有名な山の一つ」.
In formal writing, 「〜の一つである」 is common.
「一つ」 can also be written 「ひとつ」, and 「1つ」 is common in horizontal text.

daily.title: Showing off your hometown
daily.description: Showing a friend around and pointing out an old building.
daily.example: This is one of the oldest buildings in town.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: Mentioning your interests in a self-introduction.
daily.example: Cooking is one of my hobbies.

daily.title: Traveling
daily.description: Explaining a festival to a companion on the spot.
daily.example: I hear this festival is one of Japan's three great festivals.

work.title: Analysis report
work.description: Explaining in a meeting why sales dropped.
work.example: One of the reasons sales fell is the price increase.

work.title: News report
work.description: A news story introduces a social issue.
work.example: The declining birthrate is one of the major challenges Japan faces.

etymology: 「一つ」 is the native Japanese number 「ひ（一）」 plus the counter 「つ」. The pattern itself is an ordinary “noun + の + noun + だ” structure. One theory says 「最も〜の一つ」 spread through translations of Western phrases like “one of the most ...”.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: 「いちばん」 means only number one. 「の一つ」 means “one of”, without excluding the others.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「や〜など」 lists several examples. 「の一つ」 picks out just one and says which group it belongs to.

similar.title: 〜のうちの一つ
similar.explanation: 「Bのうちの一つ」 means nearly the same, but stresses “picking one out of a group”. Common in speech.

title: 〜ない〜はない (double negative)
meaning: The double negative 「〜ない + noun + はない」 means “there's no ... that doesn't ...”, in other words, all of them do. It's stronger than a plain positive.
connection: Verb ない-form + noun + は (いない／ない)

senses.label: No one / nothing that doesn't ...
senses.meaning: Rules out every exception to stress that “every ... does ...”. Use 「いない」 for people and 「ない」 for things.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + 人・もの + はいない／はない
examples: There's no one in this town who doesn't know him.
There's no problem he can't solve.
This store sells absolutely everything.

senses.label: Not a day goes by without ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ない日はない」 means “every single day ...”. Often used to stress longing, perseverance or habits.
senses.connection: Verb ない-form + 日・時 + はない／はなかった
examples: Not a day goes by that I don't think of my family back home.
There wasn't a single day she didn't practice.

notes: Don't confuse this with 「〜ないことはない」, a weak partial yes (“it's not that I can't”). This pattern is a strong, total yes.
The first half can also be a negative adjective or noun: 「この店においしくないものはない」.
The polite forms are 「〜ない人はいません」 and 「〜ないものはありません」.

daily.title: Recommending a famous song
daily.description: Telling a friend from abroad about a very famous song.
daily.example: Everyone in Japan knows this song.

daily.title: Missing home while studying abroad
daily.description: An international student writes about their feelings in a diary.
daily.example: Not a night goes by that I don't think about my family.

daily.title: Praising Mom's cooking
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about your mother's cooking.
daily.example: Everything my mom makes is delicious.

work.title: Advertising
work.description: An ad stresses how widely a product is used.
work.example: Every household in this area uses our products.

etymology: Two negatives are stacked together, and negating a negative gives a strong positive. English “there's no one who doesn't ...” works the same way.

similar.title: 〜ないことはない
similar.explanation: 「行けないことはない」 means “it's not that I can't go” and leaves room for doubt. 「知らない人はいない」 means “everyone knows” and is strong.

similar.title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
similar.explanation: 「誰も知らない」 is a total negative (“nobody knows”). 「知らない人はいない」 is a total positive (“everybody knows”).

similar.title: 〜わけがない
similar.explanation: 「わけがない」 denies a possibility (“there's no way ...”). This pattern denies that any exception exists.

meaning: 「すこしも」 with a negative means “not ... at all”, a total denial of degree or amount.
connection: すこしも + verb ない-form／negative adjective

senses.label: Degree: not at all
senses.meaning: Used with negative adjectives, or negative verbs of feeling and understanding, to say the degree is zero.
senses.connection: すこしも + negative adjective (少しも寒くない／少しも分からない)
examples: This movie wasn't interesting at all.
I don't understand what he's saying at all.
It's not cold outside at all.

senses.label: Action: not even a little
senses.meaning: Says that an action or change didn't happen at all. Often used with 「〜ていない」 or 「〜ずに」.
senses.connection: すこしも + verb ない-form／〜ていない／〜ずに
examples: I didn't sleep at all last night.
He worked without taking a moment's rest.
The town hadn't changed a bit.

notes: It must be followed by a negative: ✕「少しもおいしい」.
「少し」 alone means “a little”. Only with 「も」 does it become a total negative.
「少しも」 is slightly more formal than 「全然」. In casual speech, 「ちっとも」 is also common.

daily.title: Complaining about a boring game
daily.description: Venting to a friend about a game you just bought.
daily.example: This game isn't fun at all.

daily.title: Reassuring someone
daily.description: A friend apologizes for being late, and you say you don't mind.
daily.example: I don't mind at all, so it's fine.

daily.title: Meeting an old friend
daily.description: Seeing a friend after ten years.
daily.example: It's been ten years, but you haven't changed a bit.

work.title: Formal apology
work.description: Explaining to a client that you never meant to cause trouble.
work.example: We had no intention whatsoever of causing you any inconvenience.

work.title: Reporting on sales
work.description: Telling your boss that sales aren't improving.
work.example: Sales haven't grown at all.

etymology: The adverb 「少し」 plus the emphatic particle 「も」. 「も」 adds “not even a little”, and together with the negative it forms a total denial.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning. 「ちっとも」 is more casual; 「少しも」 also works in somewhat formal situations.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: 「全然」 is the most common and casual, and it sounds strong. 「少しも」 focuses on “not even the tiniest bit”.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: 「あまり〜ない」 means “not very”, a partial negative. 「少しも〜ない」 is a complete negative.

meaning: Thanks someone for doing something for you: “Thank you for ...”.
connection: Verb te-form + くれて + ありがとう

senses.label: To people close to you
senses.meaning: Said to friends, family and others close to you. Naming what they did before saying thanks sounds more sincere than a simple 「ありがとう」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれて(、)ありがとう (来てくれてありがとう)
examples: Thanks for coming today.
Thank you so much for helping me.
Thanks for always listening to me.

senses.label: Polite version
senses.meaning: To superiors, customers or older people, use 「〜てくださって」 or 「〜ていただいて」 followed by 「ありがとうございます」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださって／いただいて + ありがとうございます(ました)
examples: Thank you for coming despite your busy schedule.
Thank you for sending the materials.

notes: Don't say 「〜てくれてありがとう」 to a superior. Say 「〜てくださって／〜ていただいて、ありがとうございます」.
Once the favor is over, the past form 「ありがとうございました」 is common.
「〜てくれて助かった」 and 「〜てくれてうれしい」 are also common ways to express thanks.

daily.title: Birthday
daily.description: A friend remembers your birthday and sends wishes.
daily.example: Thanks for remembering my birthday.

daily.title: After a move
daily.description: Thanking a friend who helped you move.
daily.example: Thanks for helping me move. You really saved me.

daily.title: Thanking a parent
daily.description: A child thanks their mom for making lunch every day.
daily.example: Mom, thanks for always making my lunch.

work.title: Welcoming a client
work.description: Formally thanking a client who came a long way.
work.example: Thank you for coming all this way.

work.title: Thanking a coworker
work.description: A coworker helped with an urgent task.
work.example: Thanks for helping with that urgent job. It was a big help.

etymology: 「くれる」 means someone does something for me or my side, and the te-form here gives the reason. 「ありがとう」 comes from the adjective 「有り難い」 (“rare, hard to come by”): its form 「ありがたく」 changed in sound. Together: “because you did ... for me, I'm grateful”.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: 「〜てくれる」 only says someone did something for me. Adding 「ありがとう」 makes it clearly a thank-you.

similar.title: 〜てすみません
similar.explanation: 「〜てすみません」 carries an apology (“sorry for the trouble”) and is often used with superiors. 「〜てくれてありがとう」 expresses only thanks and is more direct.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただいてありがとうございます」 is a humble form, more common in business than 「〜てくださって」.

meaning: 「だろうか」 after 「のだ」 expresses the speaker wondering about something, doubting it, or asking gently.
connection: Plain-form sentence + のだろうか (noun / な-adjective + なのだろうか)

senses.label: Wondering / doubt
senses.meaning: The speaker is unsure and thinks aloud. Often used with 「本当に」「なぜ」「どうして」.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + のだろうか／んだろうか
examples: Is this really okay?
I wonder why he didn't say anything.
I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

senses.label: Polite question
senses.meaning: 「のでしょうか」 asks politely. It's softer and more courteous than 「ですか」.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + のでしょうか／んでしょうか
examples: Excuse me, does this train stop at Tokyo Station?
What should I do?

senses.label: Rhetorical question / skepticism
senses.meaning: Raises a question with doubt, hinting “probably not”. Common in opinion pieces.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + のだろうか (implying “no”)
examples: Can that method really solve the problem?
Can money really make you happy?

notes: After nouns and な-adjectives, add 「な」: 「本当なのだろうか」「学生なのでしょうか」.
「のだろうか」 is mostly for talking to yourself and for writing. To ask someone directly, use 「のでしょうか」.
「〜のではないだろうか」 gently puts forward your own opinion (“isn't it the case that ...?”). It points in a different direction from this pattern.

daily.title: Waiting for exam results
daily.description: Talking to yourself anxiously while you wait.
daily.example: I wonder if my exam results will be okay.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Politely checking with a stranger at the station.
daily.example: Excuse me, does this bus go to the station?

daily.title: Reading a science article
daily.description: Articles often open with a question like this.
daily.example: Why do people dream?

work.title: Checking with your boss
work.description: Politely confirming a deadline.
work.example: Would it be all right to submit these materials by tomorrow?

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: An editorial questions a policy.
work.example: Is this policy really effective?

etymology: A combination of explanatory 「の（ん）」, conjectural 「だろう」 and the question particle 「か」. 「の」 turns the question into an inquiry about a situation, giving the feel of “what is really going on?”.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: 「だろう」 is a guess. 「のだろうか」 is a self-directed question; the speaker doesn't know the answer.

similar.title: 〜かな
similar.explanation: 「かな」 is casual wondering with a light tone. 「のだろうか」 is more formal and common in writing.

similar.title: 〜のではないだろうか
similar.explanation: 「のではないだろうか」 means “I suspect that ...”, a gentle claim. 「のだろうか」 is a pure question or doubt.

similar.title: 〜のだ・〜んです
similar.explanation: 「のだ」 explains a situation. Adding 「だろうか」 turns it into a question about the situation.

title: 〜らしい (typical, befitting)
meaning: 「らしい」 after a noun means having the typical, proper qualities of that thing: “just like a ...”, “befitting a ...”.
connection: Noun + らしい (らしく／らしくない／らしさ)

senses.label: Typical / befitting
senses.meaning: Means something fully has the qualities expected of that noun. Usually positive. Common examples: 「男らしい」「子どもらしい」「春らしい」.
senses.connection: Noun + らしい + noun (春らしい天気／男らしい人)
examples: It's real spring weather today, isn't it?
He's a very manly guy.
What a lively, childlike picture.

senses.label: Not like ... (negative)
senses.meaning: 「〜らしくない」 means not matching how someone or something usually is or should be. Often used as “That's not like you”.
senses.connection: Noun + らしくない／らしく (adverb)
examples: That's not like you. You're usually so cheerful.
Talking like that isn't fitting for a teacher.
Study seriously, the way a student should.

senses.label: The noun 「らしさ」
senses.meaning: 「らしさ」 turns this quality into a noun: “the character / style of ...”.
senses.connection: Noun + らしさ (自分らしさ／日本らしさ)
examples: I want to stay true to myself.
This is a town with a truly Japanese feel.

notes: It looks the same as conjectural 「らしい」 (“it seems”). 「明日は雨らしい」 is a guess; 「春らしい天気」 means typical. Use context to tell them apart.
Words like 「素晴らしい」 and 「可愛らしい」 are single words, not this pattern.
The adverb form 「らしく」 means “in a way that befits ...”: 「学生らしく勉強しなさい」.

daily.title: Talking about the weather
daily.description: Greeting a neighbor on a warm day.
daily.example: It's so warm. A real spring day, isn't it?

daily.title: Encouraging a friend
daily.description: A usually cheerful friend is suddenly feeling down.
daily.example: Being so unsure of yourself isn't like you.

daily.title: Looking at a child's drawing
daily.description: Visiting a kindergarten art exhibit.
daily.example: What a lively, childlike picture.

work.title: Interview dress code
work.description: A school or company tells students what to wear.
work.example: Please come in clothing appropriate for a student.

work.title: Brand planning
work.description: Discussing product direction in a meeting.
work.example: We want to make products that stay true to our company's character.

etymology: The suffix 「らしい」 attaches to nouns to form adjectives meaning “having the proper qualities of ...”. The conjectural auxiliary 「らしい」 is generally thought to have developed from this suffix. They look the same but are used differently.

similar.title: 〜らしい (conjecture/hearsay)
similar.explanation: Conjectural 「らしい」 follows plain forms and means “it seems ...” (「雨が降るらしい」). This one follows nouns and means “having the qualities of ...”.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「っぽい」 means “a bit like ...” and is often negative or casual (「子どもっぽい」 = childish). 「らしい」 means “just as ... should be” and is usually positive (「子どもらしい」 = innocently childlike).

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 「みたいだ」 is a comparison (“like ...”, though it isn't really). 「らしい」 means it actually has the typical qualities of its type.

meaning: In casual speech, 「〜って感じ」 sums up your impression or feeling: “it feels like ...”, “kind of ...”. Very relaxed.
connection: Noun／plain-form sentence + って感じ (だ／です／の + noun)

senses.label: Summing up an impression
senses.meaning: Sums up your overall impression in one phrase. Often used with 「いかにも」 or 「まさに」.
senses.connection: Noun／plain-form sentence + って感じ(だ)
examples: This room totally looks like a student's room.
It's snowing outside. It really feels like winter now.
That shop has a stylish vibe.

senses.label: Vague / softening
senses.meaning: Adding 「って感じ」 at the end makes a statement less definite, like “that's about it”. Popular with young people.
senses.connection: Plain-form sentence + って感じ(かな)
examples: Well, I guess I just barely made it in time.
Work's been busy lately. I basically just sleep every day.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜って感じの + noun」 means “a ... that gives off a ... feel”.
senses.connection: Noun／plain-form sentence + って感じの + noun
examples: He seemed like a kind big brother.
I want to wear clothes with a grown-up look.

notes: Very casual, mainly between friends. In formal settings, use 「〜という印象です」 or 「〜ような感じです」.
「〜みたいな感じ」 and 「〜な感じ」 are also common and mean much the same.
Don't confuse it with the verb 「感じる」: 「寂しいって感じている」 means “I feel lonely”, which is not this pattern.

daily.title: Looking at photos
daily.description: A friend shows you vacation photos.
daily.example: This photo really feels like summer vacation. Nice!

daily.title: Catching up
daily.description: A friend asks how you've been, and you answer casually.
daily.example: Hmm, so-so, I guess.

daily.title: Describing a new classmate
daily.description: Telling your family about a new student in class.
daily.example: The new classmate seemed like a serious kid.

work.title: Chatting with a coworker
work.description: Talking about the new office with a coworker you're close to.
work.example: The new office is bright and feels really modern.

work.title: Informal update
work.description: Reporting progress in a relaxed team meeting.
work.example: Overall, things are going pretty smoothly.

etymology: 「って」 is the casual form of the quoting particle 「と」 or of 「という」, and 「感じ」 is the noun form of the verb 「感じる」. Together they originally meant “a feeling of ...”. In casual speech it became a set phrase for summing up impressions and softening statements.

similar.title: 〜ようだ・〜みたいだ
similar.explanation: 「みたいだ」 is for guesses or comparisons. 「って感じ」 focuses on summing up your overall impression and is more casual.

similar.title: 〜って (quotation, topic)
similar.explanation: 「って」 on its own quotes or marks a topic. 「って感じ」 is a set phrase meaning “a feeling of ...”.

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「っぽい」 means “tending to be ..., like ...”. 「って感じ」 can follow whole sentences, so it covers more ground.

similar.title: 〜がする (sensation)
similar.explanation: 「〜気がする」 and 「〜感じがする」 are more standard. 「って感じ」 is young people's casual speech.

meaning: In written Japanese, says that a phenomenon, change or trend can be observed: “... can be seen”, “... has appeared”.
connection: Noun + が + 見られる (negative: 〜は／が見られない)

senses.label: Appearing / being observed
senses.meaning: Objectively describes phenomena, changes or trends found in surveys or observation. The subject is usually an abstract noun like 「変化」「傾向」「改善」「特徴」. Common in news, reports and papers.
senses.connection: Abstract noun + が見られる／が見られた
examples: Recently, there has been a change in how young people think.
The patient's symptoms showed improvement.
This area shows a trend of population decline.

senses.label: Not observed
senses.meaning: The negative 「〜は／が見られない」 says that an (expected) change or phenomenon didn't appear.
senses.connection: Noun + が／は見られない・見られなかった・見られません
examples: Even after taking the medicine, there was no effect.
No major problems have been found.

senses.label: Can be seen (sights)
senses.meaning: Says that a certain sight, plant, animal or custom can be seen in a place. Common in travel guides.
senses.connection: Place + では + noun + が見られる
examples: In this park, you can see cherry blossoms in spring.
Rare birds can be seen in this region.

notes: This 「見られる」 isn't potential (“can see”) or passive (“be seen”). It means “naturally appears, can be observed”, and it belongs to written style.
The subject is usually an abstract noun like a phenomenon or change, not a person.
In speech, people often say 「〜がある」 or 「〜が見える」: 「少し変化があった」.
An even more formal version is 「〜が見受けられる」.

daily.title: Weather news
daily.description: A TV report on temperature changes across the country.
daily.example: Temperatures are trending upward nationwide.

daily.title: Travel guide
daily.description: Reading a description in a guidebook.
daily.example: At this time of year, you can see fireflies by the river.

work.title: Performance report
work.description: Comparing this year's figures with last year's in a report.
work.example: Compared with the previous year, there was no major change in sales.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Describing experimental results in a paper.
work.example: A clear difference was observed between the two groups.

etymology: 「見られる」 is the verb 「見る」 plus the auxiliary 「られる」. Here 「られる」 is generally considered “spontaneous”: something naturally comes into view or is observed, rather than being actively looked at.

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: 「見える」 means something is naturally visible in front of you (「山が見える」), usually concrete scenery. 「見られる」 is mostly used in writing to describe phenomena and trends.

similar.title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
similar.explanation: 「映画が見られる」 means “can watch a movie” (potential). This pattern means “a phenomenon is observed”, usually with an abstract subject.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: 「人に見られる」 means “to be seen by someone” (passive). This pattern has no one doing the action.

similar.title: 〜傾向がある・〜傾向にある
similar.explanation: 「傾向がある」 simply states that a trend exists. 「傾向が見られる」 stresses that it was found through observation, so it sounds more objective.
